paragraphs: Only the most detailed Ordnance Survey maps record the village of Gavon, in Sutherland. Perhaps it is surprising that a map on any scale should mark such a small, huddled group of huts. They stand on a bare, bleak headland between moor and sea and would seem of no importance to anyone who did not live there. But the river Gavon, on whose right bank these six chimneyless, windswept homes stand, is a geographical feature of much greater interest to outsiders. Its salmon are heavy fish, its mouth is free of nets, and all the way up to Gavon Loch, some six miles inland, its coffee-coloured water lies in one deep pool after another. If the river is in good condition and the angler reasonably optimistic, the probability of catching fish approaches a certainty. At any rate, during the first fortnight of last September I never had a day without a catch on those delightful waters. Until the fifteenth of the month, someone at the lodge where I was staying landed a fish from the famous Picts’ pool every day. But after the fifteenth, no one fished that pool again. Here is the reason why.

At this point, after some hundred yards of rapids, the river turns sharply round a rocky corner and plunges wildly into the pool. The water is very deep at its head, but deeper still farther down on the eastern side. There part of the stream turns back towards the head of the pool in a swift, dark backwater. You can fish it only from the western bank. On the eastern side, above this backwater, a great wall of black basalt rises sheer from the river to a height of some sixty feet. It must have been thrust up by a fault in the rock layers. Both its sides are nearly vertical, its top is deeply jagged, and it is curiously thin. About halfway along it, where a crack breaks its upper edge, and some twenty feet below the top, a long hole passes right through the rock. It resembles a narrow, pointed window, with a slit of daylight visible through it. Since no one would care to cast a line while perched on that razor-edged height, the pool has to be fished from the western bank. A decent fly cast will reach all of it, however.

On the western bank stand the remains that gave the pool its name: the ruins of a Pict castle. It is built of rough, barely shaped stones, without mortar, but on a large and impressive scale. Considering its immense age, it is very well preserved. The castle is circular, measuring some twenty yards across the inside. A staircase of large stone blocks, each rising at least a foot, leads to the main gate. Opposite it, on the river side, is a smaller back gate. Beyond that, a scrambling path descends a dangerously steep slope to the head of the pool immediately below. Going along it requires both caution and agility. A gate chamber, still roofed, is built into the solid wall. Inside are traces of the foundations of three rooms, and in the centre a very deep hole, probably a well. Finally, just outside the back gate leading to the river is a small platform, some twenty feet across, which has been deliberately levelled as though to support a building. Stone slabs and blocks lie scattered across it.

Brora, the town serving Gavon’s postal district, lies some six miles to the south-west. A track leads from it across the moor to the rapids immediately above the Picts’ pool. When the river is low, a man taking exceptionally long strides from boulder to boulder can cross without wetting his feet. He can then climb a steep path north of the basalt rock and reach the village. But this crossing requires a steady head and is dizzying at the best of times. The other road between Gavon and Brora makes a long detour higher up the moor, passing the gates of Gavon Lodge, where I was staying. For some vague, ill-defined reason, the pool and the Picts’ Castle had an unsettling reputation in the neighbourhood. Several times, while trudging home from a day’s fishing, I had known my fishing guide to take a fairly long way round, though heavily loaded with fish, rather than make this short cut past the castle at dusk. The first time Sandy, a strapping, yellow-bearded Viking of twenty-five, did this, he said the ground around the castle was ‘boggy’. As a God-fearing man, he must have known he was lying. On another occasion he was more honest, saying there was something uncanny about the Picts’ pool after sunset. I am now inclined to agree with him. When he lied, though, I think it was because, as a God-fearing man, he also feared the devil.

On the evening of 14 September, I was walking back with my host, Hugh Graham, from the forest beyond the lodge. The day had been unusually hot for the time of year, and soft, furry clouds blanketed the hills. Sandy, the guide I have mentioned, was behind us with the ponies. Rather casually, I told Hugh about his strange dislike of the Picts’ pool after sunset. He listened with a slight frown.

‘That’s curious,’ he said. ‘I know there’s some vague local superstition about the place, but Sandy certainly used to laugh at it last year. I remember asking him what was wrong with the place. He said he paid no attention to the rubbish people talked. But you say he avoids it this year.’
‘He’s done so several times when he’s been with me.’
Hugh smoked in silence for a while, striding noiselessly over the dusky, fragrant heather.
‘Poor fellow,’ he said. ‘I don’t know what to do about him. He’s becoming useless.’
‘Drink?’ I asked.
‘Yes, drink, though that’s secondary. Trouble led him to drink, and I’m afraid trouble is leading him to worse than drink.’
‘The only thing worse than drink is the devil,’ I remarked.
‘Exactly. That’s where he’s going. He goes there often.’
‘What on earth do you mean?’ I asked.
‘Well, it’s rather curious,’ said Hugh. ‘You know I dabble in folklore and local superstitions, and I believe I’m on the track of something stranger than strange. Just wait a moment.’

We stood in the gathering dusk until the ponies struggled up the hillside to us. Sandy, with his six feet of supple strength, strolled easily beside them up the steep slope. His long day’s walking seemed only to have half awakened the dormant power of his limbs.
‘Going to see Mrs Macpherson again tonight?’ Hugh asked.
‘Yes, poor soul,’ said Sandy. ‘She’s old, and she’s alone.’
‘Very kind of you, Sandy,’ said Hugh, and we walked on.
‘Well, then?’ I asked, once the ponies had fallen behind again.

‘Superstition still lingers here,’ said Hugh, ‘and she’s supposed to be a witch. To be quite honest, it interests me a good deal. If you asked me under oath whether I believed in witches, I would say no. But if you then asked me under oath whether I suspected that I believed in them, I think I would say yes. And the fifteenth of this month—tomorrow—is Gavon’s Eve.’
‘And what in Heaven’s name is that?’ I asked. ‘And who is Gavon? And what’s the trouble?’

‘Well, I suppose Gavon is the person—not a saint—whom we’d call the hero after whom this district is named. And the trouble is Sandy’s trouble. It’s rather a long story. But we still have a long mile ahead of us, if you’d care to hear it.’

I heard it during that mile. A year earlier, Sandy had become engaged to a girl from Gavon who worked as a servant in Inverness. Last March he had gone to see her without sending word ahead. As he walked along the street where her mistress’s house stood, he suddenly met her face to face. She was with a man whose clipped speech revealed him to be English and whose manner suggested a sort of gentleman. He flourished his hat at Sandy, expressed pleasure at meeting him, and hardly seemed to need any explanation for being out walking with Catrine. It was the most natural thing possible. A city like Inverness had its innocent social freedoms, and a girl could stroll with a man. Besides, Catrine was so openly pleased to see him that Sandy was satisfied for the time being. But after he returned to Gavon, suspicion grew like a rampant fungus in his mind. A month ago, after immense effort and many blots, he had written to Catrine, urging her to return and marry him immediately. After that, it was known that she had left Inverness, and that she had reached Brora by train. From Brora she had set off to walk across the moor, taking the path just above the Picts’ Castle and crossing the rapids to Gavon. She left her box to be sent on by the carrier. But she never reached Gavon. It was also said that, although the afternoon was hot, she wore a large cloak.
By then we had reached the lodge. Its lights shone dimly and indistinctly through the thick hill mists that had streamed gloomily down from the higher ground.
‘The rest,’ said Hugh, ‘is as fantastic as this is sober fact. I’ll tell you later.’

To my mind, a determination to go to bed is as difficult to ripen into fruit as a determination to get up. Despite our long day, I was glad when Hugh returned after hospitably handing out bedroom candlesticks. The other men had yawned their way out of the smoking room, but he came back with a briskness that suggested he was nowhere near reaching that distressing decision.
‘About Sandy,’ I suggested.

‘Ah, I was thinking of that too,’ he said. ‘Well, Catrine Gordon left Brora and never arrived here. That is a fact. Now for the rest. Do you remember a woman walking about the moor near the loch, always alone? I think I pointed her out to you once.’
‘Yes, I remember,’ I said. ‘Surely not Catrine? A very old woman, dreadful to look at. Moustache, whiskers, and muttering to herself. Always looking at the ground, too.’

‘Yes, that’s her—not Catrine. Catrine! Good heavens, a May morning! But the other one is Mrs Macpherson, the supposed witch. Well, Sandy trudges a mile and more to see her every night. You know Sandy: the Adonis of the north. Can you find any natural explanation for that? After a long day, he goes off to visit an old hag in the hills.’
‘It seems unlikely,’ I said.
‘Unlikely! Well, yes, unlikely.’
Hugh rose from his chair and crossed to a bookcase between the windows, filled with rather musty-looking books. He took a small book with a goatskin leather spine from a top shelf.
‘Superstitions of Sutherlandshire,’ he said, handing it to me. ‘Turn to page 128 and read.’
I did as he said and read.

‘September 15 seems to have been the date of what we may call this devil festival. On that night, the powers of darkness ruled supreme. For anyone who was out that night and called on their aid, they overrode the protective Providence of Almighty God. Witches, above all, were therefore especially powerful. On this night, any witch could win the heart and love of a young man who consulted her about a love potion or charm. As a result, on the same night in any following year, he would be hers for that night, even if he was lawfully engaged and married. If, however, a sudden grace of the Spirit led him to call on God’s name, her charm would have no power. On this night, too, all witches could use certain dreadful incantations and indescribable blasphemies to raise from the dead those who had killed themselves.’
‘The top of the next page,’ said Hugh. ‘Skip this next paragraph; it has no bearing on the last one.’

‘Near a small village in this region called Gavon,’ I read, ‘the midnight moon is said to shine through a particular gap or crack in a wall of rock beside the river, onto the ruins of a Pict castle. Its beams fall on a large, flat stone erected near the gate, which some people believe is an ancient pagan altar. At that moment, according to a superstition still lingering in the neighbourhood, the evil and malicious spirits that rule on Gavon’s Eve reach the height of their powers. Anyone who calls on their aid at that moment and in that place will receive everything they desire from them, though at infinite peril to their immortal souls.’
The paragraph on the subject ended there, and I closed the book.
‘Well?’ I asked.
‘In favourable circumstances, two and two make four,’ said Hugh.
‘And four means—’

‘This. Sandy is certainly consulting a woman who is supposed to be a witch, whose path no small farmer will cross after dark. He wants to find out what happened to Catrine, at whatever cost, poor devil. So I think it’s more than possible that people will be by the Picts’ pool at midnight tomorrow. There’s another curious thing. I was fishing there yesterday, and someone has set up a great flat stone directly opposite the castle’s river gate. It was dragged up from the rubble at the foot of the slope—I noticed the crushed grass.’
‘You mean the old hag is going to try to raise Catrine’s body, if she’s dead?’
‘Yes, and I intend to see what happens for myself. Come too.’

The next day, Hugh and I fished our way down the river from the lodge, taking another guide with us instead of Sandy. After landing a couple of fish there, we ate lunch on the slope of the Picts’ Castle. Just as Hugh had said, a great flat slab had been dragged onto the platform outside the castle’s river gate. It rested on rough supports that, now the slab was in place, certainly seemed designed to hold it. It was also directly opposite the narrow, pointed window in the basalt rock across the pool. If the midnight moon did shine through that opening, its light would fall on the stone. This, then, was almost certainly where the incantations would take place.

As I have said, the ground below the platform dropped steeply to the pool. Rain on the hills had made the river very high, and the water poured down in an astonishing, deafening volume, streaked with lines of greyish bubbles. But directly beneath the steep rock face on the far side of the pool, it lay black and without foam: a still, very deep backwater. Above the structure resembling an altar, seven roughly cut steps rose to the gate itself. On either side of the gate, the castle’s circular wall stood about four feet high. Inside were the remains of walls dividing the three chambers. We decided to hide that night in the chamber nearest the river gate. If the witch and Sandy met at the altar, we would hear any movement. Hidden in the wall’s shadow, we could look through the gate opening and see whatever happened at the altar or down by the pool. Finally, the lodge was a short ten minutes away by the direct route. If we left at a quarter to twelve that night, we could enter the Picts’ Castle through the gate away from the river. We would not reveal ourselves to anyone waiting for the moon to shine through the narrow window in the rock wall onto the altar before the river gate.

Night fell, very still and windless. When we slipped silently out of the lodge shortly before midnight, the eastern sky was clear, but a black continent of cloud was creeping up from the west and had almost reached the point overhead. Lightning occasionally winked from its distant fringes. Long afterwards, at intervals, came the sleepy growl of far-off thunder. Yet it seemed to me that another storm hung directly over us, ready to break at any moment. The air felt far more oppressive than such a distant disturbance could explain. To the east, however, the sky was still luminously clear. Stars embroidered the strangely hard edges of the western cloud, and the dove-coloured light in the east made it plain that the moon was about to rise over the moor. In my heart, I did not believe our expedition would end in anything but yawns. Even so, my nerves were extremely tense and raw, which I blamed on the thunder-charged air.

We had both put on rubber-soled shoes to keep our footsteps quiet. All the way down to the pool, we heard only the distant thunder and our own muffled tread. Very silently and carefully, we climbed the steps to the gate away from the river. Keeping close to the inside wall, we edged round to the river gate and peered out. At first I could see nothing: the opposite rock wall cast such a black shadow across the pool. Gradually I made out the clumps and lines of faintly shining foam that streaked the water. High as the river had been that morning, it was now infinitely fuller and more turbulent. Its deep roar filled and bewildered the ear. Only at the very foot of the opposite rock was the water completely black, without flecks of foam. That was the deep, still surface of the backwater. Then I suddenly saw something black move in the dimness ahead. Against the grey foam rose a head, then shoulders, and finally the whole figure of a woman climbing the bank towards us. Behind her walked a man. They reached the newly erected stone altar and stood side by side, silhouetted against the churned whiteness of the stream. Hugh had seen them too and touched my arm to draw my attention. So far, then, he was right. There was no mistaking Sandy’s sturdy build.

Suddenly a tiny spear of light shot across the gloom. Moment by moment as we watched, it grew wider and longer, until a tall beam, as though from a window cut in the opposite rock, fell on the bank below us. It moved slowly, imperceptibly, to the left until it shone directly between the two black figures. The flat stone before them gleamed with a curious bluish light. Then a dreadful screaming voice—a woman’s voice—suddenly rose above the river’s roar. Her arms shot up and out from her sides, as though she were invoking some power. At first I could not catch a word. Soon, through repetition, the words began to form an intelligible message in my brain. With the paralysed horror of a nightmare, I listened to a bellowing of the most hideous, unspeakable blasphemy. I cannot bring myself to record what I heard. It is enough to say that Satan was called on by every adoring and reverent name, while curses and unspeakable maledictions poured out against Him whom we hold most holy. Then the yelling stopped as suddenly as it had begun. For a moment there was silence again, apart from the reverberating river.
Then that horrible sound rose once more.
‘So, Catrine Gordon,’ it cried, ‘I command you, in the name of my master and yours, to rise from where you lie. Up with you—up!’
Once more there was silence. Then I heard Hugh beside me take a quick, sobbing breath. His finger pointed unsteadily towards the dead-black water beneath the rock. I too looked and saw.

Directly beneath the rock, a pale light appeared underwater, waving and trembling in the stream. At first it was very small and dim. As we watched, it seemed to swim upwards from distant depths and grew larger, until it lit an area of perhaps a square yard. Then the water’s surface broke, and a head appeared above the stream: a girl’s head, dead white, with long, flowing hair. Her eyes were shut, and the corners of her mouth drooped as though she were asleep. The moving water formed a frill around her neck. The figure rose higher and higher out of the current until it stood exposed to the waist, apparently shining with its own light. Her head bent over her breast, and her hands were clasped. As she emerged from the water, she seemed to draw closer. By now she was halfway across the pool, moving quietly and steadily against the great flood of the rushing river.
Then I heard a man’s voice cry out in a kind of strangled agony.
‘Catrine!’ it cried. ‘Catrine! In God’s name; in God’s name!’

In two strides, Sandy rushed down the steep bank and hurled himself into that mad swirl of water. For a moment I saw his arms flung towards the sky; the next moment he was completely gone. When that name was spoken, the unholy vision vanished too. At the same instant, a light burst before us, so blinding, and followed by a thunderclap so appalling to the senses, that I know I simply hid my face in my hands. At once, as though the sky’s floodgates had opened, a deluge fell on us. It came not as rain but as one sheet of solid water, and we cowered beneath it. There could be no hope or attempt to rescue Sandy. Diving into that whirlpool of raging water meant instant death. Even if a swimmer could have survived there, the blackness of the night made finding him completely impossible. Besides, even if saving him had been possible, I doubt whether I had enough control over my own flesh and blood to bear plunging in where that apparition had risen.

Then, as we lay there, another horror filled and took possession of my mind. Somewhere close to us in the darkness was the woman whose yelling had just turned my blood ice-cold and sent sweat streaming down my forehead. At that moment I turned to Hugh.
‘I can’t stay here,’ I said. ‘I must run—run right away. Where is She?’
‘Didn’t you see?’ he asked.
‘No. What happened?’
‘The lightning struck the stone within a few inches of where she was standing. We—we must go and look for her.’

I followed him down the slope, shaking as though I had a paralytic tremor. I felt along the ground ahead with my hands, in deadly terror of touching something human. In the last few minutes the thunderclouds had covered the moon, so no beam from the window in the rock guided our search. We groped and stumbled up and down the bank, from the shattered stone to the edge of the pool, but found nothing. At last we gave up. It seemed almost certain that after the lightning strike she too had rolled down the bank and lay somewhere deep in the pool from which she had called the dead.

No one fished the pool the next day, but men came from Brora with drag nets. Directly beneath the rock in the backwater lay two bodies close together: Sandy and the dead girl. They found no trace of the other woman.

It seems, then, that Catrine Gordon left Inverness in deep trouble in response to Sandy’s letter. What happened afterwards can only be guessed at. It seems likely that she took the short cut to Gavon, intending to cross the river on the boulders above the Picts’ pool. But we can only guess whether she slipped as she crossed and was dragged down by the hungry water, or whether she threw herself into the pool because she could not face the future. At any rate, they now sleep together in the bleak, windswept graveyard at Brora, in obedience to God’s inscrutable designs.
